items.body:
Stellar new album from Dave Sumner’s Function - arguably a sequel or sibling work to Sandwell District’s seminal ‘Feed Forward’ classic - marking his first solo LP since 2013, and best in his catalogue.

Running to 17 songs and nearly 2 hours of material, ‘Existenz’ works away from puristic, kick drum-led club tools and instead limns a sort of autobiographical story of Sumner’s relationship to techno and electronic music, all framed around a Videodrome-styled (David Cronenberg also directed the album’s 1999 namesake film) kind of occult cable TV aesthetic and strong nods to his early love of ‘80s electro.

Recorded 2016-2019, ‘Existenz’ is bound to surprise anyone who thought he just made heavy club tracks, and may well highlight his role in Sandwell District’s ‘Feed Forward’ album, which is arguably the strongest comparison in terms of their shared tone of mood, diversity of texture and structure, and, ultimately, their mesmerising effect. 

In total control of his sound, Function lures us into a labyrinthine, noirish sort of electronic thriller that embarks with the nostalgic Vangelis nods of ‘Sagittarius A (Right Ascension)’ and ends up drifting away in deeply romantic technohouse style with ‘Downtown 161’. What happens in between is primed for long headphone journeys and daily commutes, as the album weaves from spellbinding electro recalling E.R.P. to lush slow house featuring Robert Owens, to proper sci-fi electronic drones, samples of The Conet Project, and even breakbeat rollers, all interwoven with his signature acid and techno ligament and shine-eyed techno spirit.

items.body:
New from Nyahh Records - a stunning duet from Natalia Beylis on Organ and Eimear Reidy on Cello, recorded at St Georges Church, Carrick On Shannon, Leitrim on a cold early January morning with a William Telford Organ built in 1846 (reputed to be the oldest organ in ireland)...

"'Pour Upon The Sky' is a story told by the two voices of cello and organ. Influenced by the rhetorical style of 18th century vocal music, the inspiration for this piece came naturally to Eimear who has a background in early music and has performed alongside the organ in a variety of settings from chamber works to Bach's larger orchestral works such as St Matthew Passion. In 18th century music, the cello & organ perform a role as continuo players. Traditionally the cello and organ are both intertwined and interdependent, playing the bass line and harmonies together and providing a foundation for the rest of the ensemble while soloists come in and out.

In 'Pour Upon The Sky', Eimear and Natalia play within and without of this traditional form. Freed from the need to hold the solid ground for an ensemble, the cello and organ playfully explore the space as they pass the role of solo and continuo back and forth.

TRACK 2/SIDE B: 'The Whistling Dust' is a slow steady study of the microscopic flutters of the organs and the organ. The heart of the Telford rattles and breathes as the cello dances in and out. When Natalia & Eimear began working on these pieces in the cold January, the Telford, which seemed like it had been sitting quietly for quite some time, shook and trembled as its insides were awoken. 'The Whistling Dust' speaks to the moment when the instrument moved alive, every opened stop knob of the pipes bringing the feel of the microsounds of the machine closer and closer as the cello offers utterances of encouragement."

items.body:
Mutual, leading prism-pushers Batu & Dozzy break fresh ground on duo debut ‘Exhale’, encompassing a spectra of tempos, moods & grooves in pursuit of elusive studio geists between Dozzy’s Rome facility and Batu’s peripatetic CPU.

Seeded in an ad hoc b2b DJ set at Draaimolen Festival, ’23, and cultivated over sessions at Dozzy’s hardware treasure trove in Rome, ‘Exhale’ naturally calibrates the two operators’ distinct visions on eight cuts teeming with detail and clean-hoofed for club use. Dozzy’s quarter century of obsessive, finely variegated techno tekkerz elide Batu’s signature offbeat syncopation and feel for texture within deceptively effortless designs that arguably transcend the sum of their parts. The results surely pin-point a dancefloor ideal of cyborganic sensuality and chromed out chronics that references the now, the future, while exerting mercurial sidespins on tried & tested forms.

In the artists’ own words: "It was interesting to see Omar interacting with my studio methods," explains Dozzy. "I know my machines very well. It was fun to do something out of my routine and use my machines in a different way to turn on Omar's ideas. There were a few things I was very excited to use, especially with someone who's an expert and used these instruments for a very long time," Batu reveals. "We tried lots of different tempos, different rhythmic patterns. I was excited by the direction we were taking, and getting so many ideas of where it could go."

In combination they generate a slew of rudely balanced equations, tentatively toeing glassy waters in the hyaline cavern of ‘Emergence’, locking into a swingeing Afro-acid churn on ’Spiral’, and stepping  to more angular, holographic techno on ‘Drift’, with nods to the nuance of mbalax-via-oingy boingy dubstep in ‘Off Axis’. And it only gets craftier in the 2nd half, diffusing the finest haze of cyberdub FX and palpitating subs on ‘Swarm’, training tendons to the tightest steppas techno on ‘Flicker’ and the title tune’s expansive trek, before seeing it off with a sublime update of early AI electronica in the shine-eyed swoon of ‘Bloom’.

items.body:
Shakali practises signature forms of overeasy exotica on a second jag with NNF, after a gem for Good Morning Tapes, rummaging thru the ambient undergrowth between Spencer Clark fantasias, Japanese environmental and modal spiritual jazz.

"Finnish multi-instrumentalist Simo Hakalisto makes mosaic music of strings, bowls, bells, reeds, wind, water, and obscure electronics, threaded in subtle currents of color and texture. The title of his latest, Toinen Luonto (Finnish for “second nature”), alludes equally to Shakali’s earthen, tactile soundworld and Hakalisto’s deepening comfort with his craft.

The album’s eight songs feel coaxed as much as composed, a web of resonances set in motion and allowed to simmer, build, or billow. Vibrations and silences unspool and intertwine, alternately pointillist and diffuse, attuned to some hidden harmony of the spheres.

In addition to his own repertoire of rare instruments (including a 36-string kantele, built by Hakalisto’s grand-uncle), several notable collaborators contributed to Toinen Luonto: saxophonist Julian Overall; Hakalisto’s partner in the duo Lunar Horns, Timo Juntunen, playing udu and percussion; American experimentalist Roy Werner; and Belgian ambient flute samplist Les Halles."

items.body:
Alex Zhang Hungtai pivots yet again on 'Orion/Mother', playing (mostly) trumpet alongside some of the New York City underground scene's most intriguing improvisers, including Kwami Winfield, Laura Cocks, Lester St. Louis, TAK Ensemble's Madison Greenstone, 75 Dollar Bill's Che Chen and Leo Chang.

 'Orion/Mother' has its roots in a set of home recordings Zhang made with some of his talented local friends; "playing with you all deeply informed my current understanding in improvisation," he explains in his thank you note, "without you this album would not have existed." So over a two week period, in a rehearsal space in New York, he invited a handful of his friends to start "an ad-hoc group", playing trumpet over chopped up home recordings and wrenching them into the future. And while the finished article - split into two distinct sections - is long, it's fully worthy of your attention. As always, Zhang brings a unique ear into the room, resisting any usual improv tropes to concentrate on sounds that most artists would avoid - unruly resonances, glitches, off-piste rhythms and unsubtle interferences.

At it's best, the record sounds like jazz specters vanishing thru faded noise remnants and the wreckage of lost experiments. On 'Shadow Integration', Zhang's brassy wails echo out over a slippery, semi-rhythmic drum machine pattern, and on 'Tanhäuser Gate', the trumpet is even more isolated, weeping over a muted soundscape that's credited simply as "Ableton" on the accompanying notes. He maintains the same energy when he's working side-by-side with his collaborators, too, finding space for Winfield's circuit bent belches on 'Nataraja' and Chen and Chang's percussion on the jaw-droppingly spannered opener 'Sidewinder'. And even when the tone shifts on 'Mother', heading into a lighter (comparatively at least) zone on the woodwind-heavy 'Kali', Zhang has a knack for tying everything together with his lyrical performance. Just peep the title track, almost seven minutes of uncanny clanks and Tōru Takemitsu-strength murmurs that Zhang butters with pure improvised emotion.

items.body:
Potent, lysergic lounge music and psych-fonk-exotica out of Brussels, with Michael Crabbé letting everything slosh out of the lines in a real slow burn head melter, like Spencer Clark meets Giulio Erasmus and Pekka Airaksinen on some vintage Hoffmans. Another wyrd doozy from Antwerp’s reliably off-the-wall label, Souvenirs From Imaginary Cities.

“Straight from the weedy fields of swampville Bruxelles we bring you 8 ‘tranches de vie’ of deep zone-hall by weirdtronic bass veteran Michael Crabbé’s best fitting sound costume to date: the mighty Rudi J! You might know him from earlier outfits but that’s not the main issue here. Rudi J is!

When this swamp thing touches the pads, it’s off-road after three seconds, even if you’re in the middle of Europe’s capital. Mixing analog dirt and digital sound bits in a very loose and personal take on dancehall, we’re pretty far away from the dance floor but definitely swinging. It’s a trippy affair wandering around concrete flowers with a deep ambient flavor, but it’s edgy.

A hot summer fever dream following his own lusty path, full of life and wonder but with something sinister hiding around every corner. Often reaching for the stars, a deeper shade of bass keeps things nicely grounded. These sounds are built with a sound system in mind and bass culture at heart. Even if you can definitely surf on it from your couch, picking out all of its ear-pricking details, it will very much come alive on a big sound.

A layered affair with almost jazzy and orchestral elements peeping through the stereo-field, spectral and dissonant but also playful. Like early dubstep, some of these tunes can destroy a clubsound, keeping you skunking out in pedestrian mode and snorting up the atmospherics, finally forgetting about that damn phone.”

items.body:
Back by demand - 2nd hand copies are known to trade for triple figures - Cindy’s timeless suite of sexy, hazed dream-pop is acutely tipped to anyone who holds a flame for Julee Cruise, Voice Actor, Lynch, Enya, Bianca Scout, Vince Clarke...

‘I’m Cindy’ is a chef’s kiss of effortlessly slow, seductive lo-fi songwriting that practically smushes earlobes with its heavenly marriage of Kai Hugo's faded production lustre and singer, Blue LoLãn’s range of whispered sweet nothings and harmonised coos. In the years since its original release it’s taken on a life of its own as a go-to succour for lovers of blissed-out, cinematic waft with equal measures of soft-focus, nostalgic FM synths and details that caress and crack in all the right, tender places. 

Conceptually derived from Palmbomen II’s ‘Memories of Cindy’ session of 2017, the 13 tracks find marbled whorls of sensual fascination within that LP’s fantasy reminiscence, here expanded into a spectrum of LA-via-Antwerp dream-pop like Johnny Jewel meets Alex Zhang Hungtai on the synth and sax pearl ‘Another’ or lip-smacking cruiser ‘Justin’, thru a Voice Actor-esque ‘Voice Message’ and the gossamer FM synth fronds that wrap it up on ‘Maybe Because It’s Over Now’, whilst secreting shimmers of Vince Clarke ballads in ‘2y & 6m’, and acid-laced lo-fi machine crack shades away from Maria Minerva on ’Never Let Me Go’.

No brainer!

items.body:
Real heart-stopping, life-affirming, almost indescribably beautiful posthumous album featuring (for the first time) vocal works by beloved, dearly departed, Ethiopian nun and now-legendary pianist/composer Emahoy Tsege Mariam Gebru, room recorded straight to tape between 1977-1985, sounds of life just about audible in the background. Almost had an out of body experience listening to it the other night - just a perfect, 10/10 album.

’Souvenirs’ is an intimate self-portrait written, recorded and compiled by the late Emahoy Tsege Mariam Gebru; a classically-trained pianist turned nun, whose singular style of jazz and blues-inflected composition and performance became globally renowned in her latter years via reissues and compilations reaching as far back as the 1960s, namely the ‘Éthiopiques 21: Piano Solo’ CD and a much-prized eponymous set in 2016. At the age of 99, Emahoy passed away in Jerusalem last year, whilst planning towards this first ever showcase of her vocals - which have never appeared on her purely piano-based recordings until now, making for a truly life-affirming experience from its opening bars. 

The posthumous release, realised in collaboration with Emahoy’s family and Mississippi Records - is a stone cold stunner. It grants unprecedented access to her discrete craft and inner world in Addis Ababa, against a backdrop of the Ethiopian Red Terror and Civil War, prior to her subsequent exile in a Jerusalem convent. Whilst all no doubt defined by her signature, intricate and lilting type of classical meets jazz-blues phrasing, the eight songs are all far more concise than her usual instrumental works, made even more spellbinding by the revelation of her softly contoured and captivating vocals that beautifully trace and overlie the cadence of her keys. It’s just pure, unbridled expression that’s only heightened by the seemingly off-the-cuff nature of the recordings, as if she just sung the songs to herself, impromptu, never intended for public consumption.

Replete with incidental creaks of the piano stool, birds outside the window, and Emahoy’s finger on the record button, the songs depict themes of loss, mourning and soon-to-be exile, sung into a basic boombox. They place us in the room with her, closer than ever, privy to a vocal version of the closing number to her eponymous compilation, now unveiled as a dedication her niece, the titular Tenkou, with lyrics to guide her adulthood “Don’t cry / Childhood won’t come back / Let it go with love”, alongside the beatific, open-window paean ‘Clouds Moving on the Sky’, and melancholic hiraeth of ‘Ethiopia My Homeland’ or ‘Don’t Forget Your Country’, and ineffable, humbling elegance of idea and execution to ‘Is It Sunny or Cloudy in the Land You Live?’ and ‘Where is the Highway of Thought?’.

Unmissable.

items.body:
¿DONDEDOS, Pascual Martinez and Jeremy Castillo, release Drifting Nowhere via Rubadub

"¿DONDEDOS is young dude/unc duo hailing from the Mission. Pascual Martinez (young dude) and BPT head honcho Jeremy Castillo (unc) have spent the last few years in the stu, cooking up this deep fried, groovin' 4 tracker. Fans of 2011-16 LIES and Future Times releases, “Biology" era Young Marco, Juju and Jordash, and the Wah Wah Wino crew are in for a treat.

In an era where literally every aspect of dance music is overly programmed and manicured, ¿DONDEDOS take a massively refreshing approach marked by true experimentation. All drums were recorded on the Roland R8, and the melodies were live played with a loose, jammy feel not felt on many electronic 12" releases in 2026. They're a jam band baby!!!!! 

The fun starts with "Drifting Nowhere," a fried oddball deep house record with one of the year's most infectious basslines. Be ready for it to be on a loop in your brain long after the track has stopped playing.

2nd track "Dies Varos" was described by BPT fam Izaak from Loveshadow as sounding like "part of the Mediterranean touching Mexico." Ahhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhh. (that was a deep relaxed sigh, not a scream for once!!!)

"Music for Patios" sounded pretty good on a walk and not on a patio so, just FYI, only a suggestion not a requirement. 

Ender Noche Caminando features Diego Herrera (AKA Suzanne Kraft) on sax. In Jeremy's own words, this track features "oddball dancehall drums on the R8 with 80s synth pop dub melodic sensibilities." "

items.body:
More gold from Japan’s endlessly curious Em Records, this time shining a light on southern Californian post-minimalist composer Jeff Bruner, highlighted by Visible Cloaks’ Spencer Doran and bringing together stunning works spanning 1978 - 2020 for mbira, calypso dub and fretless gut-string banjo - huge tip FFO Richard Crandell, Terry Riley, Roland P. Young, Takoma, General Strike, Daniel Lentz.

"I first came across Jeff's mysterious "Reggae Foes" 45 in the mid-2000s at the legendary Logos book/record store in Santa Cruz, California (RIP) - the kind of generic sleeve and label that gives you nothing more than a font and some scant shards of text to go by (luckily this text was "A Flying Saucer Came Down and Burnt My Baby's Neck"). What I heard upon bringing it home felt like some kind of alternate-timeline post punk calypso, unknowingly adjacent to the deconstructions occurring at the Black Ark or in David Cunningham's early productions. When I finally talked to Jeff many years later, I was even more surprised to learn that he was also entrenched in southern California's post-minimalist composer scene in the 1970s alongside many of my compositional heroes, work which this compilation presents for the first time. Couldn't think of a better place for it to be transmitted from than EM!" (Spencer Doran/Visible Cloaks)

Four Corners is a compilation that showcases the various facets of American West Coast minimalist composer Jeff Bruner, with pieces from the 1970s to the 2020s displaying a cohesive set of aesthetic concerns. Bruner has a kinship with the composers Harold Budd and Daniel Lentz, the latter being a mentor to Bruner, and one can hear a relationship with the music of other minimal/post-minimal composers such as John Adams and Terry Riley. 1979's "Magic Mbira", a key piece in this collection, particularly highlights a Riley-esque element, and with its skillful use of tape delays reminiscent of Lenz's cascading echo system. Bruner and his mbira piece also have musical affinities with Roland P. Young and his classic Isophonic Boogie Woogie, in their shared melodic and structural concerns, as well as a desire to perform their compositions in a wider range of performance spaces, away from traditional recital halls. Another side of Bruner is revealed in the funhouse-mirror "Reggae Foes", a deconstructionist post-punk calypso-reggae tune and skewed Black Ark filtered through Cunningham/Toop's General Strike. The remaining two pieces are melancholy beauties of solo instrumentation: "Cold Rain and Snow" is a fretless gut-string banjo re-imagining of an American folk song; "Remembrance in a Pale Room" is a lovely piano piece dedicated to Lentz. Bruner has built upon a tradition, altering and adding to it with his individual vision, giving us this collection of intriguing and beautiful music. Available on CD/Vinyl/Digital, with E/J liner notes by Jeff Bruner, rare photos & the score for "Magic Mbira"."

items.body:
New LP from French-born, London-based composer and musician Pascal Bideau via Tonal Union.

"Cartographers and US multinational technology corporations might think they’ve mapped out most of our big, beautiful blue planet, and yet there’s always more to discover if you know where to look. French-born, London-based composer and musician Pascal Bideau takes this as his central premise on a new album of intrepid sonic exploration that delights in the sensation of being somewhere you’ve never been before. ‘Terra Incognita’ invites us to seven faraway sonic imaginariums fusing global and spiritual jazz with life affirming minimalism into a hypnotic, polyrhythmic odyssey.

This time, the albums’ sound palette is more vibrant, earthy and abundant, drawing inspiration from the radiating optimism and high-energy sources heard in Afrobeat, Highlife and Electronic Afro-pop music, sounding looser, free and primarily interested in raw sensations. Antithetical to the precise ostinatos and gamelan patterns of the acclaimed debut ‘Fleeting Future’ (2022) and ‘Lines’ (2023). Terra Incognita, then, is a hybrid blend of traditional music and modern electronics, a trip into the unknown that ambulates freely, taking pleasure in its repetitions and never staying still. Bideau suggests this unmarked territory could be as much a fantasyland as it is a transportive journey into the inner self."

items.body:
Adrian Rew's properly hypnotic cult classic 'Slot Machine Music' has finally been reissued and it sounds even more terrifying and prescient than it did back in 2013 at the height of the basement noise era. One of the best environmental recording records bar none - don't sleep.

Back in 2009, PAN released its fourth album, 'Kenrimono', a set of recordings made by Greek sound artist Ilios at Japanese pachinko halls. The sheer density of it was as shocking and as intense as anything the noise genre had to offer, packed out with whirring, crunching and chiming resonances that took you to the smokey epicenter of the Japanese gambling world. And when 'Slot Machine Music' arrived a few short years later we assumed the sound would be similar; we were wrong. Initially dropped via Rew's own Ergot Records on CDr before the great Aaron Dilloway stepped in to handle the vinyl edition on his own Hanson imprint, the album seemingly grew from the Midwestern noise petri dish - but it wasn't an exercise in aesthetic posturing, using the racket of the modern American casino to mimic the intensity of a Wolf Eyes set. Instead, Rew was drawn to the experience itself, that's been meticulously designed by malign forces to guide behavior: those trapped inside the casino's four walls are seduced into spending more, losing more and returning to do it all over again.

Rew didn't know much about the environment when he visited Cleveland's Horseshoe Casino for the first time in 2013 armed with an Olympus LS-11 recorder and a camera. And over four months, he developed a peculiar relationship with the culture, surreptitiously taping the soundscapes at various Midwestern locations - in Michigan, Indiana, Ohio and Illinois - while attempting not to lose too much cash in the process. And it's a warts-n-all set, with dialog snippets and outdoor ambiance giving us more than simply the dense mass of chimes and stings and themes that you'd hear on the casino floor itself. What Rew is able to do is create a snapshot of a time and place, capturing the sheer desolation of the casino experience and using it to drive a narrative that Robert Altman would be proud of. The first thing you notice is that each machine's sounds are in tune with the next; "game designers," explains Rew, "tune their machines to the key of C in order to optimize harmonic cohesion." So although Rew's recordings are full-bodied, they're never too chaotic or discordant. 

Indeed, if you check in for the entire record - 2013's iconic 'Slot Machine Music' and its 2014 sequel 'Slot Machine Music Vol. 2' - you'll be lulled into the same false sense of security that entrances casino regulars. It's almost like ambient music, packed out with tiny sonic details that some well-paid sound engineer-cum-neurologist worked for years to figure out. Guided meditation music? New age crypto-psychedelia? It's all here, packaged in neon-lit one-armed-bandits aimed to target the dopamine centers of aging boomers with money to burn. And the best thing about the recordings is that Rew keeps some of the chatter intact, so we can hear him tangling with casino security, or haggling with his slot machine neighbors over change. We can hear the cheers and claps as paltry sums are won while vast fortunes are lost. The best moment for us comes when Rew wanders outside Grand Victoria Casino in Elgin, Illinois at the dead of night, the crickets singing as the machines echo from behind grand double doors. A freight train rushes past and blots out any other sound, distorting the recording.

It's a good reminder that although you might be able to hide from reality inside the casino, the Midwest will inevitably confront you with its rusted truth.

items.body:
Collaborative LP from Bristol mainstays Sam Binga & Addison Groove.

"Bristol's Sam Binga & Addison Groove have been friends and collaborators since their 2013 'BS3' EP, released on Modeselektor's '50 Weapons' imprint. This project, the third full-length on Binga’s Pineapple Records, is born from an intense 72-hour session at the legendary Devon Analogue Studios, where the pair were able to explore their mutual love of uptempo machine funk - whether that be Detroit Jit, Chicago Boxjams or Turbo Electro.

Three days of intense creativity across classic drum machines, vintage analogue synths and rare hardware effects resulted in a collection of raw but powerful audio building blocks - and over the past two years, the pair have been gradually shaping them into what is now a complete project - the BAGS INC album. Across 12 tracks, Binga & Addison explore that exciting space between 140 and 150 bpm - but while it's fast, it's not 'hard'; as you'd expect from the creators, it's still got that wiggle, and the all-important cheekiness for which they're known."

items.body:
Heavy-lidded, late nite jazz-soul suss from the keenly touted Ugné Uma & producer emer, secreting a dozen sleepwalker specials on their duo debut with Stroom. FFO Leila, Lolina, ML Buch, Tirzah, Voice Actor.

Hashed out in imaginary air between Brussels and Berlin, ‘You and Me’ projects a mutual dream sequence of downbeat stardust and midnight jazz vapours supposed by two emergent figures of the EU undergrowth: one Ugné Uma paying up on the promise of her single for Somewhere Press, plus Marija Rasa’s emer, still fresh from a standout solo debut LP on Short Span in late ’25. In duo, they reaffirm, double down, and transcend the sum of their parts with a classy grasp of sandman tekkerz, suspending bodies between duvet-dive beatdown and hypnagogic soul with a slow-burn frisson of romantic intimacy.

With no hard edges or surprises for the supine mind, the album unfolds in its own liminal space with a gauzy sense of daydreamy-into-nocturnal physics. The filigree dub of emer’s ‘Fog’ LP is found dialled down to more powdery ambient jazz and soul smoulder, and inflected with a fine-wrought R&B discipline that ideally swirls Uma’s classic, smoky delivery, to the natural extent that it feels like they’ve been cooking together for years. Dusted but not dusty, it all treads the finest line of classic and modernist late nite needs for the ages, and especially hot, sleepless hours.

items.body:
On the eve of the release of her debut album, 2017's   Take Me Apart  , Kelela offered a state of the union for Black queer musicians. "Every time you are challenging power, you're met with this notion that you're going to lose opportunities," she  told  an audience in a SOAS University lecture hall. "It takes a while to figure out how to push, in terms of imposing your way on others. It's the only way you can actually feel good. Because the default setting is created for white men, and perhaps in this day and age, Black men, to succeed."

With the arrival of her third album,  new avatar , she has every reason to feel good. Few artists have imposed their will on the underground and mainstream as effectively as Kelela.  Take Me Apart  and the feverishly awaited follow-up, 2023's   Raven  , stacked vocals as expertly as the Beach Boys or Brandy, then shot them through experimental club beats that put the break in heartbreak, and washes of ambient that soothe both body and soul. The latter was  Resident Advisor 's album of the year for a reason.

But Kelela's restlessness, first signalled by a series of  remix   albums  travelling through various dance floor landscapes, only intensified: just when you thought she'd be the torchbearer for, say, stark Aaliyah-coded R&B or Björkian-slanted pop, she'd pivot and release a jazz album.  The Blue Light , recorded live at New York's legendary Blue Note club, where she'd drive from her home in DC for weekend sojourns, was a triumph.

On  new avatar , she's put down the harp and picked up the axe. Her timing, as usual, is prescient, with Charli xcx's  turn toward guitars  on the horizon and  rumours  of Beyoncé completing a trilogy through a reclamation of the rock legacies of Sister Rosetta and Tina Turner. Kelela, though, sounds more like she’s been listening to Black innovators like A.R. Kane. Unlike the dozens of new bands who are building signal chains to summon shoegazers past, however, she's conjuring the genre's blister and burn to shake off, not lose herself in, all of the noise. 

Lead single "idea 1," for example, unfurls tangled ropes of guitar and scratchy blankets of bass. Her vocals gather force as they ruminate, linking in tone and timbre with the guitar lines. "Building it up, tearing it down, where are we now?" she wonders. The guitars shift into overdrive, and so does her voice, hotter and meaner than ever before. "Bearing your cross, it's your loss," she sneers. If this is her shoegazing, it's because she's getting them ready to kick your ass.  

So maybe she's not feeling  that  good, but she's sounding better than ever. The first half of  new avatar  leaps over emotional landmines detonated by controlled bursts of noise. "Crystalize" showcases what happens when Kelela lets her voice rip, and what happens when she uses consonants like a guitar pick on a string. The effect is epic balladeering, complete with gated, crashing drums reverb'd enough to remind us that Cocteau Twins were making power ballads just as hard as Whitney Houston. 

"Outta Time" enlists A.K. Paul for some computer blues. Across a chasm defined by lonely handclaps, a chiming guitar lick or two and a bone-rattling drone, the pair mourn the distance between them. Kelela goes first: "Don't cut me off / See, now you really fucked up," she warns. For his part, Paul groans his way into a verse she keeps interrupting. "We're touching eternity," he pleads, but her hands are waving goodbye and the track ends in a swirl of echoes, going in circles, just like they are.

 new avatar 's second half returns to the rhythms Kelela has pushed forward for much of her career. But if "Don't Piss Me Off" and the PinkPantheress-assisted "The Bridge" build soft power through UK garage clicks, they're also riding on dream pop's ecstatic currents. "The Bridge" is especially epic, telling the story of two people building a queer courage for themselves with a soundtrack that builds a bed of murmurs and warm smears of synth strong enough to make the risk worth it. "New Life," made with Fousheé, also maps out femme desire, this time in a glittering slow jam. The track is engineered to be pure swoon; more pop should sound this effortless.

Kelela knows this, and wants us to know she knows it, too. On the roiling "Point Blank," which surfs church bells and a killer bassline across crashing funky breaks, she puts power on notice: "The more I pour, the more you reap / Got me working while you're fast asleep." Not for long, though.  new avatar  is what all that work paying off sounds like, and she's not waiting around for the rest of the world to catch up. Clutching onto a very Joni-coded bassline on closer "If We Meet Again," and clock the  if , she lays it out simply: "You don't try hard enough / You don't rock hard enough." Fair enough. Nobody's rocking harder than Kelela right now.

items.body: It was only a matter of time. In the cosmology of our music, one thing was certain: the orbits of Thelonious Monk and [Ahmed] were destined to overlap, after having crossed in the name of Ahmed Abdul-Malik, Monk's bassist in the late 1950s quartet, heard on 1958's Thelonious in Action and Misterioso , as well as on the album with John Coltrane at Carnegie Hall unearthed in 2005. Pat Thomas (piano), Seymour Wright (alto sax), Joel Grip (double bass), and Antonin Gerbal (drums) "make music about (Note: bear in mind this "about" because is the key to almost everything) Ahmed Abdul-Malik, they excavate, re-inhabit, and use a-new the now overlooked documents and fragmentary plans of his mid-20th-century synthetic vision to produce a new jazz imagination for the 21st century. [Ahmed] and Abdul share a critical engagement with time, specifically in challenging its linear trajectory and offering sites and modes of synthesis and rupture instead. In their music, fragments of time are scattered and re-arranged in the present". So says the band's official statement, which theoretically should explain everything. Theoretically. Malik (1927-1993), son of Caribbean immigrants, was a NYC bassist, oudist, composer, educator and philosopher, he played with Art Blakey, Earl Hines and Randy Weston and his albums Sahara (1958) and East Meets West (1960) fused aspects of Arabic and East African musics and thought, his committed long-term relationship with Sufi Islam and then-modern jazz and thinking, in revolutionary and vital way. But, as well as honoring these traditions, Malik's straddling, synthetic and inclusive vision is one of the great projects of imagination in jazz. He mixed sounds and ethics, meanings and beliefs in open, experimental ways, without any dogma and this became the true north for [Ahmed]: to visit and re-think his compositions and the process potential in them. This is why we emphasized the adverb "about": neither covers, nor lab experiments in cold musical eugenics; neither free jazz, nor classic (even two super skilled listeners and reviewers like Lee and Fotis, in past reviews, scratched their heads between amazement and ecstasy) but a hypnotic Black Monolith that has cast an enigmatic and fascinating shadow for some years, writing a new chapter destined to remain in the Annals of Music. From the very first time we heard them, the immediate reference for us, rather than the music, was the cubist painting, in which we found all the elements expressed by [Ahmed] and vice versa: the break with traditional perspective; the geometric decomposition; the simultaneity of views; the reduced color palette and the use of collage. Art must not portray reality but interpret it, like a cognitive tool, as per cubists’ First Commandment, and Pat Thomas & co. are exactly abiding by that. After 6 albums, (all excellent but “Giant Beauty” and “[Sama’a] (Audition)” are two real, unmissable, t-rex carnivorous records) and a 7-inch, here finally, after having engaged with Monk’s standards in various individual or collective ways, the hesitation is broken and [Ahmed] “Play Monk”: when a title says it all. In 2 CDs recorded in March 2025 at Fish Factory Studios (the same “Sama’a” recording sessions), with a cover photo of the legendary pianist at Fisherman’s Wharf in San Francisco, portrayed by the lens of Baroness Pannonica de Koenigswarter that alone is worth the purchase of the album, 6 standards (“Bye-Ya/Epistrophy,” “Friday Thirteenth,” “Round Midnight,” “Epistrophy,” “Evidence,” “Oskar T.)” are atomized in the particle accelerator, “transforming each composition into a shifting quantum time artifact. The melodic, harmonic, rhythmic, and spatial gestures of each piece become complex vernacular forms, creating a dialogue in time and a (red)shifting lens through which to view our material present. Into the fissures of Monk’s form, [Ahmed] pour their own play, colliding and dancing with Duke Ellington, Cecil Taylor, Caribbean diasporic music, European improvisation, and Jah Shaka in their pursuit of future music,” to borrow Otoroku’s notes. Too much? If you trust just a little bit in your humble writer: NOT.AT.ALL. As usual, they set out and ride pedal to metal, no self-indulgence or self-referential (or falsely free-form) rotating solos, but a “wall of sound” that Phil Spector would have liked to produce, where more than playing the notes, they use them and the ideas in and about them, as a vehicle for their unique imagination, moving from what they know into new uncharted, creative lands. It’s too easy to predict that this album will take no prisoners in our end-of-year Top Tens, but it’s even really hard to imagine what other albums will live up to it. We’d like to close with the words of the great Luke Stewart, certainly much more titled than us, in expressing a reflection on Abdul-Malik and [Amed]: “The journey of self-discovery, communing with the eternal sound. A musician steeped in multiple worlds; oceans apart yet closely connected in ancestral memory. Musicians such Abdul-Malik were able to experience the global community of sound warriors, drawing inspiration from ancient cultures to support personal investigation. The connection was made clear, the music of Africa would certainly influence the African in America despite the atrocities of the Middle Passage, chattel slavery and continued racist violence that sought to sever any connection to the continent. The beauty of Malik’s investigation is this original fusion of new music (Jazz) of the African in America with ancient music of Africa. It is a shining example of collaboration in culture, where the music is allowed to shine for itself. This is the inspiration that is being tapped, being explored in this collaboration where rhythm is the basis for the sound. Just like Malik, [Ahmed] allow the spirit of the collective push the sound as the music develops into exalted chaos. Joy Be Upon Us!”I Play Monk by أحمد [Ahmed] Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body:
When LNGSHOT arrived at the NBA Rising Stars Invitational 2026 in Singapore, they were stepping into a space built for a different kind of rising star. The event brought together young basketball talents from across the region, but for LNGSHOT, it was also a chance to meet a new crowd — one that may have come for the game, but left with a first impression of the group.

Speaking to Bandwagon at the tournament, the members reflected on what they share with young athletes: pressure, ambition, discipline, and the need to keep going even when the journey looks different for everyone. They also opened up about basketball dreams, what they would want to learn from the players, and why Jay Park remains one of their biggest sources of inspiration.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Bandwagon Asia | Music News • Asia Festivals & Artists (@bandwagonasia)

The NBA Rising Stars Invitational is all about celebrating the next generation. As artists who are also at the start of your journey, what message would you like to share with the young athletes competing here?

WOOJIN: We actually got to meet the Korean team earlier today, and… I don’t know, there’s something about meeting people from your home country when you’re overseas that makes you feel connected to them, even if you’ve never met before.

But not just the Korean players — seeing athletes from so many different countries giving it their all has been really inspiring. I hope every one of them succeeds someday.

Everyone reaches their goals at a different pace, so I just hope they keep working hard and stay in it for the long run. That’s something we need to do too.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Bandwagon Asia | Music News • Asia Festivals & Artists (@bandwagonasia)

Many people here may be discovering LNGSHOT for the first time because they came for basketball. When you’re performing for a new audience like this, how do you hope to leave a lasting impression?

RYUL: I just hope people remember us as a group that’s full of energy, vibrant, and has a really unique charm.

If you had the chance to exchange advice with the young athletes competing here, what’s one thing you’d like to learn from them, and what’s one thing you’d hope they could learn from you?

LOUIS: Something I’d like to learn from the players? Probably… proper shooting form. I’d really like someone to teach me.

WOOJIN: Honestly, you really do need to learn.

LOUIS: I don’t think you’re the one who should be saying that… Everyone here is so good at basketball. I’ve always dreamed of doing a dunk, so maybe one day I’ll be able to show you guys.

OHYUL: You’ll definitely be able to do it soon.

WOOJIN: Personally, if there’s one thing I could teach the players, it’d be how not to grow any taller. That’s probably the only thing I can help with.

OHYUL: That’s true.

WOOJIN: Go to bed late…

OHYUL: Right.

WOOJIN: …And don’t eat too much.

The tournament celebrates rising stars from across different backgrounds and countries. Is there someone whose journey has inspired LNGSHOT, whether in music, sports, or another field, and what about them has stayed with you?

WOOJIN: I think definitely Jay Park, because he chose us and, in a way, he’s the person who gave us the life we’re living now. Whatever the question is, my answer is always Jay Park.

LOUIS: He’s our CEO but, I mean, even if he’s our CEO, he kind of feels more like a dad to us, so we’re always looking up to him. He always teaches us stuff.

Like what you read? Show our writer some love!

items.body:
Japanese music heavyweights have come together for an ambitious new cross-genre collaboration. Awich, CHICO CARLITO, ONE OK ROCK, and Paledusk have officially unveiled YAO, a new collective that bridges hip-hop, rock, and alternative music, making its debut with the release of the explosive single '777' alongside a cinematic music video.

Serving as the group's first release, '777' brings together the distinct styles of all four acts into a genre-blurring track that reflects YAO's mission of pushing creative boundaries. The project was born from a shared desire to create something that transcends genres, generations, and artistic conventions.

The accompanying music video, directed by Hidehito Hotta, places the members against a post-war-inspired landscape of damaged buildings and abandoned vehicles. Shot on a cinematic scale, the visual turns scenes of destruction into a symbol of unity, resilience, and collective strength—echoing the project's central message.

YAO traces its origins to a joint performance by ONE OK ROCK and Awich, where conversations between frontman Taka and the rapper about working together eventually evolved into a larger vision. The project later expanded to include CHICO CARLITO and Paledusk, bringing together artists from across Japan's hip-hop, rock, mainstream, and underground scenes.

Named after the Japanese concept of "Yaoyorozu," which celebrates the coexistence of countless spirits and perspectives, YAO aims to champion collaboration through diversity and creative exchange.

items.body:
Tyrell Dub Corp Dials Up The Latter Bit In Dub Techno On 'MK618'

8 July 2026

Perhaps it is from experiences like collaborating with increasingly popular techno act Shaun Moses within the live duo MO/SS or a natural progression, but Sanil Sudan is definitely dialling up the second word on dub techno, the genre he has dedicated his moniker Tyrell Dub Corp to, on 'MK618'.

The new EP by the Delhi-based artist revs up the tempo for the first 2 tracks. Still carrying the expanse of dub and synth chords bouncing around unobtrusively, the opener 'Inner Garden' is one of the more percussive outings under the TDC banner. The rigid drum groove contrasts against the limber harmonic layers, and if there is a hook beyond the repeating bassline, it's in the interplay of analog tom sounds.

Even the succeeding title track gives the drums a more prominent role, as their mercurial echoes provide the only thing tactile in the engulfing yet elusive pumping atmosphere. Only on the final 'Drift' does the pace slow down and the textures get more easily traceable. They step out from the expanse as individual characters evolving noticeably to allow the hypnotic constantness of a bassline looping beyond the rhythmic framework and a mangled vocal sample repeating like a chant. With that, 'Drift' sets itself apart from the more cloud-like nature of the rest of the EP.

Listen to 'MK618' below and follow Tyrell Dub Corp for more information.

items.body: There is something fitting about Vittorio Guindani finding a home for these recordings in Vilhelm Hammershøi’s The White Door. Before becoming an album, La Porta Bianca existed in a kind of limbo: music without a place, waiting for the image that would finally give it a context. Originating from the same 2023 sessions as Materia Breve, these pieces ultimately found their symbolic shelter in Hammershøi’s painting, whose silent rooms and atmosphere of suspended time resonate deeply with Guindani’s own aesthetic. In recent years Hammershøi has become something of a cultural touchstone, the epitome of understated cool: endlessly reproduced in design magazines and social media feeds, his empty rooms and half-open doors offering a vision of stillness that feels increasingly fabricated. Yet La Porta Bianca reaches beyond mere aesthetic affinity. Guindani adopts the painting not simply as an image but as a conceptual space, a luminous threshold through which these abandoned recordings can finally enter and find their place. The connection with Materia Breve is deeper than chronology. That album was accompanied by Luca Lanfredi’s poem Il richiamo del nome, whose recurring images of thresholds, absences and elusive presences seem to resonate strongly with Guindani’s artistic vision. Lines such as “Every universe has its own language” and “Every universe is a music score” feel particularly relevant here. Guindani has often spoken of sound not as narrative but as presence, of his desire to remain on the threshold before form solidifies into meaning. La Porta Bianca inhabits precisely that liminal territory, where sounds are allowed to simply exist rather than signify. If Strame was, in Guindani’s own words, “a collection of ashes,” shaped by fear, loss and the collapse of certainties, La Porta Bianca occupies a more contemplative register. These are still fragments and residues, field recordings reduced to their barest essence, loops that hint at melodies without fully resolving, small sonic events enlarged until their grain becomes visible. Track 05 (none of the tracks have titles) is particularly revealing, subtly recalling the ambient dub sensibility explored in more recent releases such as Wabi. Here, however, echoes and resonances are stripped of any stylistic excess and reduced to pure spatial relationships. Like Hammershøi’s painting, the album is not concerned with what lies beyond the door, it doesn’t try to second guess. Sometimes it’s enough just to be there, to be present in the moment, to stand before the door. The result is one of Guindani’s most understated and affecting releases: a work of quiet attention where silence becomes a form of presence, and every small sound seems illuminated by a soft light from an adjoining room. It is fitting that the album’s graphic restyling by Vittorio Guindani places a “white door” over Marina Marcolin’s artwork for Materia Breve. We choose to view any reference to Jonathan Barnbrook’s design for David Bowie’s 2013 album The Next Day, which superimposes a large white square over Masayoshi Sukita’s photograph from Heroes, as intentional. To expand on the production process for La porta bianca we’ve reached out to Vittorio Guindani. La Porta Bianca gathers pieces left aside from the Materia Breve sessions and places them under the sign of Vilhelm Hammershøi’s The White Door. What changed when you revisited these recordings? Did the painting help you understand what kind of place these sounds belonged to? As is often the case for me, I only find the meaning of things once they have already been made. The material left aside from Materia Breve has been the subject of repeated listening on my part from 2023 until today, and I often found myself wondering what to do with it. I considered—and still consider—these pieces worthy works, so I wanted to give them a home and a name. In situations like this, I need a spark of inspiration. Whether it comes from a poem (Strame, for example, is a word drawn from the writings of Montale), a text (as was the case with Jisei in 2020), or a philosopher matters little. The discovery of Hammershøi filled that gap. In his paintings, I found again the quiet, silent atmosphere that surrounded me during the making of Materia Breve, the sense of emptiness I needed. The White Door is both the perfect painting and the perfect title: a luminous, uncluttered opening that seems to say to these orphaned pieces, “Come in, you are home.” Looking at Materia Breve (2023), Strame (2025), and La Porta Bianca (2026), one senses a continuous investigation into fragments, remains, traces, and impermanence. Do you see these works as part of a larger cycle, and what has this long exploration taught you about listening and loss? Absolutely. I believe my entire sonic exploration has been a development of these themes. Listening has taught me how to bear witness. This became especially clear through the practice of field recording: finding myself in front of something immense that I cannot control and of which I can only be a witness. In this sense, I have found affinities with various aspects of Zen Buddhism, such as non-attachment and, consequently, the ability to let go—things that are far easier to understand than to put into practice. The loss of my parents between 2020 and 2024 has undoubtedly influenced the way I perceive things. You have described Strame as “a collection of ashes” shaped by feelings of fear, impotence, and the desire to react through the ruins. La Porta Bianca, by contrast, feels quieter and more reconciled. Has your relationship with absence and fragility changed in recent years? La Porta Bianca and Materia Breve both date from 2023, during the post-Covid resurgence, positioned midway between Jisei (2020), which was deeply infused with Zen influences, and Strame (2025), my most dramatic work. Humanity seems closer than ever to catastrophe; we are hanging by a thread, fragile and defenceless. The collapse of civilisation and the violent arrogance of our times—so evident for all to see—have led me toward a profound disillusionment, pushing me to search for meaning amid this absurd climate. You often describe yourself as being interested in creating a presence rather than music. Could you elaborate on that distinction? What qualities make a sound become a presence? Sound and Presence are undoubtedly connected. Sound is the material of inquiry from which I begin—full of possibilities—allowing me to shape a Presence before it becomes a completed Form. What interests me is remaining on the threshold that precedes the narrative implied by Form: creating something that simply is, without any apparent meaning, something that does not demand attention. Paradoxically, I love to think that what I do is of no importance. Both Materia Breve and La Porta Bianca use numbered titles rather than descriptive ones. Is this a way of resisting narrative interpretation and encouraging a more direct encounter with sound? I’m also reminded of Luca Lanfredi’s poem accompanying Materia Breve, particularly the lines “Every universe has its own language” and “Every universe is a music score.” Do these ideas resonate with the way you think about your pieces? Words close things off; they define boundaries and impose limits. For this reason, I prefer not to give titles unless it is strictly necessary. I think this is also why I love poetry and its peculiar use of language, as can be seen in Luca’s beautiful text. I deliberately never asked myself what it might mean (it was written after listening to the pieces), yet I find the passages you highlighted deeply resonant, especially when connected to the idea of the soundscape—a foundational concept that has always animated my work. Your work often sits between field recording, sound art, reductionism, and composition. Looking back from Jisei through Strame, Materia Breve, Altri Steli, and La Porta Bianca, do you feel your practice is becoming more minimal, or are you simply learning to listen more attentively to what was already present around you? At the beginning, my approach was more landscape-oriented, whereas now I often focus on smaller, more “interior” sounds, isolating their content like individual grainy frames. I have listened a great deal and gathered a vast amount of material, and now I simply manipulate and organise it according to a certain element of chance—or rather, according to an instinct that has been refined over time. Removing, reducing, and stripping things away allows me to explore sound in its infinite possibilities. At the moment, I am recording very few new sound sources. I no longer find much interest in the sounds around me that I have not already documented in one form or another. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Yorkshire producer Jinjé built “Give A Pluck” from a series of live modular takes, running sequencer patterns through two synthesis voices and twisting the patches in real time until the track’s central riffs came into shape. Jinjé is the solo project of Lee J Malcolm, the Leeds producer who founded Vessels, a band that started out in post-rock and reworked itself into a live techno outfit. He fed evolving sequencer patterns through the pair and recorded a run of improvised takes, twisting the patches in real time, then cut and reshaped the strongest passages in the studio into the darting riffs that drive the track. His work on London label Earthly Measures has long drawn on afrobeat, afro-folk and highlife recordings from the sixties and seventies, and that thread runs through “Give A Pluck”: a choir of children singing in a tribal style carries over from “Kush”, the track before it on the EP, anchoring the modular arpeggios to something older and warmer. The single arrived on 22 May ahead of Traces & Tremors, Jinjé’s five-track EP for Earthly Measures: his first solo record on the imprint after releases with Mesh, Ostgut Ton and his own Making Friends. items.body: Review by Caph — I picked this album up not knowing much about Jordsj� beyond a vague sense that they belonged to the current wave of Nordic folk-prog acts, and Pestkr�nikene turned out to be a genuinely rewarding listen from start to finish.What struck me most is the guitar work. Several passages here feature twin-guitar harmonies that reminded me immediately of classic-era Wishbone Ash ? that same interlocking, melodic dialogue between two guitar lines, weaving around each other rather than one simply carrying the lead. I wasn't expecting that kind of British '70s harmony-guitar approach to show up in a Norwegian folk context, but it fits naturally into the songs rather than feeling like a stylistic quotation.Beyond that, I found the songwriting more disciplined than a lot of records in this genre tend to be. Folk-prog albums can drift into vague atmosphere for its own sake, but here the quieter, almost medieval-sounding verses build into fuller arrangements in a way that always feels purposeful. The production has a warm, slightly weathered character that suits the "chronicle" concept behind the album, and the vocals stay restrained enough to let the guitars, keys, and rhythm section carry much of the melodic and emotional weight.I've gone back to this record several times now, and each listen has revealed a bit more detail in the arrangements, especially in how the guitars trade off. For anyone who enjoys melodic, harmony-driven guitar work layered over Nordic folk atmosphere, this is well worth seeking out ? the Wishbone Ash comparison is one I'd stand behind, and it's part of what makes this album stand out from its peers.A strong, well-crafted release that I'd recommend without hesitation.

items.body: Review by alainPP — Muse's 10th epic opus?arriving after a thirty-year career?propels the listener into space at the speed of sound amidst colorful, cinematic atmospheres, oozing prog-rock vibes reminiscent of an uninhibited Queen. It spans ballads, hard rock explosions, symphonic space rock, art-rock, and decadent neo-classical pop-opera with a retro 1977 signal."The Dark Forest" features Eastern synths, soaring violins, cinematic neo-classical orchestration, and spellbinding, theatrical vocals. It delivers muscular rock with heavy riffs and an electro tone worthy of a Ghost-style black mass?*Sanctus*. With a cinematic feel and Queen-esque melancholic guitar, the die is cast, and there is no escape. There are echoes of Rossini and "Knights of Cydonia"; the 55-person choir commands attention, as does the London Metropolitan Orchestra on strings. "Nightshift Superstar" is an airy blend of electro-pop and dub-dance?the kind of thing a grumpy prog purist would hate, especially given its TV-friendly appeal. It channels Daft Punk, driven by Chris's killer bassline, vocoded vocals, and disco-infused synth pads?a sure-fire hit for 2026. "Shimmering Scars" offers a piano-and-vocal ballad with a bewitching, introspective lament from Matt; the *Interstellar*-esque space organ elevates the track further, shifting into catchy industrial pop before bathing us in a melting, cloud-like guitar solo. "Cryogen" opens with the sound of a speeding vehicle?part car, part plane?and a dissonant, signature guitar riff. Matt goes full-on madcap rock-opera, with a riff that slices through the air, showcasing the band's hard-rocking power. "Be With You" pays homage to Queen with its solemn, melancholic organ and a dynamic mix of melodies that keeps the listener constantly engaged. That velvety?almost robotic?electro keyboard sound, reminiscent of radio-friendly Muse, translates perfectly here. The bass, the splashing drums, the guitar that whinnies?it's a moment of pure pleasure, perhaps less inspired but richer in harmony; a perfect, theatrical mini-prog track.Then comes 'Hexagons,' featuring a shimmering, arpeggiated, and distorted guitar solo; you can easily picture this torrent of notes live. Dominic floods this grandiloquent track with his drumming. The vocals are spellbinding, the synth hypnotic, the mood solemn?it's enough to make your blood run cold. It's a precision-engineered space-rock sound with cascading notes, sweeping you into a bottomless cosmic odyssey that straddles the line between rock and the ultimate slow dance. A powerful finale?Muse is back?segueing into a distorted pulse that launches 'The Sickness In You & I' straight into the stratosphere with a heavy rockabilly vibe. It's dreamlike, balancing a hard-rock riff against danceable vocals that wouldn't be out of place in the few remaining nightclubs. There's an electro rhythm, a driving beat, and a building frenzy reminiscent of Suicidal Tendencies. The metallic riff delivers a shock?if such a thing is still possible?so get dancing; prog is breaking new ground here. We headbang through an apocalyptic finale of fiery electro notes that usher in 'Unravelling,' the conclusion to this sublime triptych. Matt, backed by minimalist synths, starts off like a ballad before shifting into Olympian djent-metal. It's a perfect blend of hard-rock groove and sugary vocals, with breakdowns heavier than Metallica's leading to an orgasmic peak?simply irresistible. Next is 'Hush,' featuring a White Stripes-esque vintage riff, prominent backing vocals, and a piano-driven beat?modern prog-rock at its finest. It mixes rock and pop-dance, with Ellie's whispered vocals frolicking over crystalline keyboard melodies. Matt adds an 8-string rock riff to keep the fans hooked; Simple, beautiful, and musical, with a spacey outro that drifts into the ambient, despair-laden 'Space Debris'; Matt agonizes over his lyrics in this heart-wrenching folk ballad, where the organ's lingering resonance amplifies his pain?a reminder of his divorce. The orchestral string finale evokes Kwoon?perfect for this style?while a 55-voice choir adds further emotional depth. A metaphorical track about the need to cherish and nurture Life.Muse delivers a sequence of tracks that smash open the doors to modern prog: 9 and 13 minutes of pure madness, leaving vast sonic spaces for the instruments to breathe.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — The sensational avant-prog collective black midi announced an indefinite hiatus in 2023, allowingband members to focus on side projects, solo ventures, and what have you. Frontman Geordie Greep wasthe first to come up with a solo project - the ecstatic 2024 album 'The New Sound', originallyreleased on Rough Trade, the label responsible for releasing all of black midi's studio albums.Greep is joined by Seth Evans here, a frequent collaborator of his former band, as well as drummerMorgan Simpson, an ex-bandmate. A cast of additional musicians are credited with individualcontributions to different songs, but the core of this album was composed by Greep and Evans, in anattempt to continue exploring the vividly satirical narratives that had become the norm for blackmidi. Influenced by a wide range of styles, Greep's songwriting is one of the more impressiveaspects on 'The New Sound', an album rooted in the complex and unconventional sound of black midi,while incorporating elements of art rock, jazz-rock, Latin rock, and even samba.And while this album is not necessarily a conceptual record, a common theme that unites the majorityof the narratives here is desperation. Greep's protagonists are these pitiful, lonely men who happento be incredibly alienated and insecure, which by itself provides for some excessively comicalscenarios that are definitely worth exploring. Musically, 'The New Sound' is by far the mosteclectic exercise to have come out of the black midi camp, and Greep's daring fascination withBrazilian popular music, jazz-rock, and Latin rock, has allowed him to forge some truly brillianttracks. Opener 'Blues' introduces a chaotic but technical guitar arrangement that probably ties thisalbum to preceding black midi releases, while the following track 'Terra' is a more appropriatepresentation of the so-called "new sound", with its delicate bossa nova undertones. The terrificsingle 'Holy, Holy' marries the sophisticated prog pomp and the jazzy leanings of this record quiteseamlessly, while its twisted lyrics give an excellent overview of the album's general thematicdirection. Prancing around the thin line between obnoxious and brilliant, we are offered some denseand dissonant rock pieces like 'Walk Up' and 'Motorbike', both of which explore some visceral avant-garde ideas. At the same time, this album has no shortage of nuanced jazz-rock compositions, such as'Through a War' and the dreamy 12-minute-long suite 'The Magician', which is quite different fromthe rest.'The New Sound' is a wild album that is surprisingly more accessible than any preceding black midirelease, and when you combine this with its bold eclecticism, this entire LP becomes an extravagantride through Geordie Greep's limitless fantasies.

items.body: Review by arcane-beautiful — The self titled album from My New Band Believe is a great debut from the project spearheaded by former Black Midi member Cameron Picton. An interesting foray into the worlds of prog rock mixed with chamber pop, art rock and experimental music, it is overly pastoral at times, as if the material itself was recorded in Canterbury in the early 70s. Musically fantastic, the overall guitar work really stands out, with lovely acoustic work that is akin to Steve Howe's playing in Yes's glory years. Cameron's vocals also show range and emotion than he did with Black Midi, but at times it does come off as very Dan Bejaresque. A great debut which hopefully is a path to future material. I'd give this a high 7 to low 8 out of 10. The track I'd recommend is Love Story.

items.body: Review by Matti — Here's a purely pragmatic approach to this 10 cd box set. That is, I won't be dealing with the albums themselves at all, but for your pleasure or convenience I can list them: Roxy Music (1972), For Your Pleasure (1973), Stranded (1973), Country Life (1974), Siren (1975), Manifesto (1979), Flesh + Blood (1980) and Avalon (1982), with the 9th and 10th CD's containing "Singles, B-Sides and Alternative Mixes". I will concentrate on the overall physical delivery, its pros and cons. First, the box's physical size is very handy. Often the multi-CD boxes are very big, but this is not much taller than the regular CD size. I prefer it that way.Each studio album is represented in a two-fold cardboard sleeve, in their original cover art, without any extra prints or bonus tracks. Visually the package is gorgeous: you can lay in front of you both front and back covers of all albums and cherish their fancy cover designs, often featuring a woman or women. The relatively poor cover art of the poorest Roxy album Manifesto has mannequin dolls.Then the negative side: since there are no supplementary booklets or anything, and since the CD size is notably smaller than the original vinyl size, some texts are very hard to read, especially on Country Life where the tiny gold-coloured letters become badly unvisible against the green trees. Some kind of a supplementary booklet or leaflet could have contained at least track titles with track numbers and lengths, even if there wasn't any further information on the band and the albums, which of course would be ideal and much appreciated. The lack of information severely concerns the 2-disc set of single cuts and alternative mixes. Six single-released songs have two different mixes. Actually I must confess I haven't properly listened to these two discs yet; I expect the non-album B-siders to have a rarity/curiosity appeal at least. If I'm not mistaken, there are nine non-album tracks (including the well-known John Lennon cover 'Jealous Guy').For anyone wanting to listen -- perhaps for the first time like me -- to the complete studio output of the legendary art-rock/sophisti-pop band, this box set is very useful. If you already have several of the eight albums, it may not be that necessary.

items.body: Review by Matti — After their fifth album Siren (1975) Roxy Music went hiatus for a few years and returned with Manifesto (1979) that I found surprisingly dull, containing very unmemorable song-material, when last week I listened to it and several other RM albums entirely for the first time. Here in PA this seventh album is ranked almost as low as Manifesto, but to me it's definitely much stronger, approaching the sophisti-pop excellence of Avalon (1982), which was my one and only Roxy Music crush in my early teenage years.By now Roxy Music was basically a trio of Bryan Ferry on vocals and keyboards, guitarist Phil Manzanera, and Andy Mackay on saxophone & oboe. Produced by Rhett Davies and recorded with session musicians, this album was a commercial success (No. 1 in the UK), but the reviews were pretty mixed, nor has the album become a classic like Avalon. It's nowhere near equally good, but I can imagine that had I listened to this one instead, it just might hold a special place in my listening history. [Just for fun I share a delightful scene in the lovely 90's drama series Cold Feet: Adam buys the CD, moved by nostalgia, and later, having come across his old flame, he sees in his mind's eye both his ex and present sweetheart on the album cover.]The album starts with a cover of a 1965 Wilson Pickett song 'In the Midnight Hour'. It's OK, nothing more though. The rest of the A side was entirely written by Ferry. 'Oh Yeah (On the Radio)' reached UK top 5 as a single, like the album-preceding 'Over You' had done. I sincerely like it as a light-hearted, finely produced pop tune with an uplifting chorus. 'Same Old Scene' I remember hearing as a kid, and thus to me it shares the same nostalgia with the mentioned following album. The synth oriented soundscape is not quite as sophisticated, but as a song per se I could imagine it being in Avalon as well. The title track, just like the previous PA reviewer points out, is a bit monotonous but graced by a really cool bass line. The sensual and hypnotic 'My Only Love' is among my RM favourites. Excellent interplay of keys and guitar, plus an economic sax solo, not to mention the gradually matured, seductive vocals of Bryan Ferry (whose parodic vibrato on the earliest RM albums I can hardly stand!).In comparison 'Over You' sounds surprisingly average. 'Eight Miles High' is the album's second cover song, originally by The Byrds from 1966, and definitely more interesting than the Pickett tune. The Ferry composition 'Rain Rain Rain' is quite monotonous but I like it more than the title track. The final two tracks Ferry co-wrote with Manzanera. A highlight track 'No Strange Delight' has a nuanced arrangement and a fascinating atmosphere. Enjoyable 'Running Wild' is a slow-tempo ballad, partly slightly reminding of 'Avalon'.Not all songs are winners, and the production lacks the finesse of Avalon, but to me this is clearly the second best RM album, and I round my 3� stars up despite the lack of any prog essence. Definitely pretty high on my list of the best pop albums from 1980.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Remembering the future is really just looking at the past, isn't it? It is a matter of interpretation, much like the content of this conceptual work, which tells the story of an extraterrestrial named Bluebird. Bluebird communicates with a blind child, sharing knowledge about human evolution, the origins of Earth, and humanity's destiny; the child's unique ability suggests that understanding and feeling may be more important than what is seen, which is often confusing and deceptive. Things are not what they seem, and despite a cover that promises a wild, crazy world..."Remember the Future - Part I" truly seems to begin during the latter part of the title track, featuring a guitar solo accompanied by organ that evokes freer, wilder times. It also brings to mind the astral journeys of the Welsh band Man, who had also dabbled in the Krautrock sound in the past. "Confusion," its final section, truly dives deep into the ocean and breathes something other than oxygen; Roye Albrighton's guitar plays, yet also cuts and stings, followed by Allan "Taff" Freeman's distinctly progressive keyboards.The same applies to the second part, (Remember the Future - Part II) and upon reaching "Tomorrow Never Comes", the third section within it, it is Roye's guitar notes that draw us into labyrinths that shift from the spiral of a snail shell to the labyrinth of the inner ear.Some notes were reminiscent of David Gilmour, before ending with a strong Doobie Brothers vibe in Let It Grow. The iconic cover was created by Helmut Wenske, also known by the alias Chris Hyde, a German illustrator and musician who had also designed A Tab in the Ocean in 1972.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — "Un druide est giboyeux lorsqu'il se prend pour un neutrino" is the opening track of the second album by the French quartet Pryapisme; unable to settle on a single genre, they play them all?simultaneously. Much like Naked City, yet distinct, given their French origins and strong symphonic leanings, they weave together a hybrid of electronica, hardcore, jazz, space rock, industrial, and, of course, progressive music.There is a touch of video game sound, and with it, electronic music and psychedelia, that fits perfectly into that highly elastic, cultivated subgenre comprising diverse influences; this makes for an intriguing prospect when seeing them live.It is pure Krautrock infused with classical piano, maintaining a captivating, infectious rhythm, whether in complex time signatures reminiscent of King Crimson or the progressive electronica style of John Digweed.Random Jean Vigo continues to blend electronica with classical and, later, distinctly rock influences; it's like Daft Punk turning into Rick Wakeman and then Metallica... all coming together in the end. Once again: you'd have to see that live!"La notion de chiralit� de spin..." kicks off with a free-jazz vibe, featuring a layering of saxophones and the yowling of the guest cat "La Belette," alongside a guitar that alternates between violence and a highly solemn keyboard. If you aren't familiar with this fabulous quartet, you should start listening with "Lesbian Bordello," as that one-minute-forty-eight-second track rounds out the picture. "J'ai envie de te claquer" plays like a horror-tinged Nouvelle Vague parody, making even Frank Zappa look tame, while the genre-hopping continues, shifting from funk to TV themes as if channel-surfing... but on the radio.When they play jazz, as in Cochenille, membrane et volcanologie, they make it gritty and street-style, like something out of a film noir or the way John Zorn used to play back when he still played the sax, but then, atonal keyboard notes combined with percussion create a truly spellbinding kind of fugue, turning this entire contemporary blend into a genre unto itself."Jon-bon-jon-boutros-boutros-boutros-bovi-miou-miou" is worth it for the title alone... but it also features music with a deep, deep keyboard, so deep it takes on an Eastern progressive vibe, to the point where it sounds like Ryuichi Sakamoto is behind the keys, experimenting all over again."Je suis venu, j'ai vu, j'ai sagouinu" is a progressive hardcore funk track featuring numerous complex cuts and breaks, as well as jazzy trio-style digressions and explosive bursts of energy that blow the song, and the �lbum, wide open; indeed, when the piano is left playing solo, it sounds as sophisticated as Zappa during the Hot Rats era."La nuit sur le Mont-Chauvelu" sounds like a heavy metal orchestra doubling as a classical choir, incorporating fragments of classic horror themes, such as Mussorgsky's Night on Bald Mountain. It truly demonstrates their ability to go classical and epic, while also reimagining the material across genres ranging from heavy metal to jazz and Stevie Wonder-esque funk. The guitar work is serious, and throughout the album, the rhythm holds steady as the listener keeps pace with a musical carousel that promises plenty more spins, as many as a cat makes before settling down to sleep.

items.body: Klar haben The Beatles geniale Pop-Hits, revolutionäre Studiotechniken und weltweiten Ruhm – aber haben sie auch Soul? Dieser Frage ging das legendäre Label Stax aus Memphis, Tennessee nach und ließ die Crème de la Crème der eigenen Stars Beatles-Songs covern. Diese Versionen zeigen nicht nur, welch großen Einfluss die Fab Four auf ihre damaligen, auch genrefremden Peers hatten, sondern auch, wie gut »Hey Jude«, »With a Little Help from My Friends« und andere Klassiker mit fetten Bläsersätzen, Background-Chören oder inbrünstigem Soul-Gecroone – etwa in Otis Reddings Version von »Day Tripper« – funktionieren. Denn natürlich zeigt sich, dass selbst vermeintlich totgespielte Songs durch diese Soul-Interpretationen überraschende neue Facetten gewinnen. Für diese Einfach-Vinyl-Edition wurde die ursprüngliche Tracklist von Stax Does the Beatles um fast die Hälfte auf die wahre Essenz eingedampft. Deutlich fokussierter tauchen nun sowohl die Interpreten als auch die gecoverten Songs jeweils nur einmal auf. Ausgewählt wurden Highlights wie die monumentale, fast zwölfminütige »Something«-Interpretation von Isaac Hayes, David Porters wilde Gitarren-Version von »Help« oder die zarte Live-Aufnahme von »Yesterday«, die eindrücklich zeigt, warum Carla Thomas als Queen of Memphis Soul bekannt ist. Dass die Wertschätzung durchaus auf Gegenseitigkeit beruhte, beweist übrigens ein Brief von George Harrison, in dem er den Otis-Redding-Produzenten Jim Stewart 1966 überzeugen wollte, das Beatles-Album Revolver in den Stax-Studios aufzunehmen.

items.body: Erinnerung an die eigene Endlichkeit gefällig? Glenn Undergrounds Klassiker Atmosfear hat inzwischen 30 Jahre auf dem Buckel. Der Deep-House-Blaupause, die Meilensteinen von etwa Larry Heard in nichts nachsteht, hört man das nur insofern an, als sie vor Pioniergeist und Experimentierfreude strotzt. Dieses Album betrat weitestgehend unerforschtes Terrain und brachte seinerzeit unorthodox zusammen, was auf den ersten Blick nicht zwingend zusammengehörte: Seetaucher-Samples mit kräftigen Bläsern, langes, freigeistiges Klavierspiel mit Synths aus der »Washing Machine« und, wohl am wichtigsten, griffiges, analoges Drumming, das jeden Anflug von ziellosem Muckertum im Keim erstickt. Atmosfear trifft so ziemlich die Mitte zwischen dem seriösen Tiefgang von Mr. Fingers und der Aufgekratztheit eines Paul Johnson und weiß, wann auf Samples von Analoginstrumenten zu verzichten ist – man höre nur den Maschinenfunk von »May Datroit«. Im Anschluss folgt der Überhit des Albums: Über »Colouration« hinweg antworten sich simple Fünf-Key-Akkorde, während im Hintergrund Pads wie Rauchschwaden auf- und abebben – simpel, aber effektiv. Wer diesen Track hört, weiß auch 2026 sofort, was Deep House bedeutet: Unmittelbarkeit, Glückseligkeit, Geborgenheit. Und natürlich kreative Basslines wie auf »Dance Slam«, die wie eine Penrose-Treppe keinen Anfang und kein Ende zu haben scheinen. Glenn Undergrounds größte Leistung ist es wohl, all diese Zutaten über die komplette Albumlänge hinweg zu einer Einheit verschmolzen zu haben.
